title: Sharding and distributed databases
scopeHtml: Scope: sharding, 2PC, Raft, Spanner and CockroachDB, NoSQL families, LSM vs B-tree, CAP, when to leave Postgres.

notes.title: Why leave a single node
notes.html:
One Postgres node, scaled up, goes surprisingly far. You split the data only when one machine can no longer hold the write rate, the data size, or the availability and latency you need.

Rough ceilings (illustrative, workload dependent): a well-tuned 64-core, 512 GB RAM, NVMe Postgres handles tens of thousands of simple transactions/s and a few TB comfortably. Pain starts when: writes exceed one machine's WAL/fsync capacity, the working set no longer fits in RAM, vacuum and migrations on multi-TB tables take too long, or you need users in different continents to write locally.

Ladder, cheapest and most reversible first:

  1. Indexes, query fixes, connection pooling.
  2. Bigger machine (vertical).
  3. Read replicas and caching.
  4. Table partitioning on one node.
  5. Functional split (move a service's tables to its own database).
  6. Sharding the same table across nodes (hard, mostly one-way).
  7. A natively distributed SQL database.

Worked example. 20 TB, 30,000 writes/s peak, 99.99% target. Partitioning by month keeps each partition ~200 GB so vacuum and index builds are quick; a functional split moves events away from accounts; only if one hot table still outgrows a node do you shard it.

Industry examples. Instagram sharded Postgres by user/media ID with logical shards mapped to physical servers. Notion sharded its Postgres by workspace ID (reported: 32 then 96 logical-to-physical shards). Stack Overflow ran a few large SQL Server boxes for years.

Decision gravity. Steps 1 to 5 are reversible; step 6 is a one-way door because every query, join, transaction and migration must now know about shards.

Everyday analogy. A shop: first reorganise shelves, then get a bigger shop, then hire more cashiers, and only then open separate branches that each stock different goods.

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to sharding at 100 GB.
  • Not distinguishing partitioning (one node) from sharding (many nodes).

notes.title: Sharding: strategies and shard keys
notes.html:
Sharding splits one logical table across many databases (shards), each holding a subset of rows. The shard key decides which shard owns a row.

Strategies:

  • Range: user_id 1 to 1M on shard 1. Good for range scans; risk of hot spots (all new users on the newest shard).
  • Hash: hash(user_id) % N. Even load; range queries become scatter-gather; changing N moves most data unless you use consistent hashing or many logical shards (e.g. 1024 virtual shards mapped to 8 hosts, so adding hosts moves whole virtual shards).
  • Directory/lookup: a mapping table says which shard has tenant X. Flexible (move big tenants), but the directory is a critical dependency.

Shard-key rules: high cardinality, even distribution, and the key that appears in most queries so each hits ONE shard. Per-tenant SaaS: tenant_id. Social: user_id.

-- Citus-style example: distribute a table by tenant
SELECT create_distributed_table('orders', 'tenant_id');
-- colocate related tables so joins on tenant_id stay local
SELECT create_distributed_table('order_items', 'tenant_id', colocate_with => 'orders');

What gets harder. Cross-shard joins, global unique constraints, cross-shard transactions (next section), schema migrations across N shards, resharding, and global ordering/auto-increment IDs (use Snowflake-style IDs or ULID/UUIDv7).

Worked example. 4 TB users data, target 500 GB per shard: 8 shards minimum; choose 64 logical shards on 8 hosts (8 per host) so growing to 16 hosts only moves logical shards, with no rehash of rows. Hot tenant? Lookup table moves tenant 7 alone to a dedicated shard.

Industry examples. Vitess (YouTube, Slack, GitHub on MySQL), Citus (Postgres extension, now in Azure Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL), Pinterest's early MySQL sharding with IDs embedding shard numbers.

Everyday analogy. A phone book split into volumes by surname letter (range) or by a hashed number (hash): lookups by surname hit one volume; "everyone called Anna" hits all.

Common interview traps.

  • Picking a shard key that skews (country, or a celebrity user).
  • Forgetting that secondary indexes on non-key columns require scatter-gather.
  • Auto-increment IDs per shard colliding.

notes.title: Two-phase commit and its problems
notes.html:
Two-phase commit (2PC) lets several databases commit one transaction atomically. A coordinator runs: Phase 1 PREPARE (every participant makes the transaction durable and votes yes/no, promising it can commit); Phase 2 COMMIT (if all said yes) or ABORT.

Coordinator        Shard A        Shard B
PREPARE ---------->  yes (durable)
PREPARE ------------------------> yes (durable)
(write decision to coordinator log)
COMMIT ----------->  done
COMMIT ------------------------>  done

Postgres supports it with PREPARE TRANSACTION 'gid' / COMMIT PREPARED 'gid' (needs max_prepared_transactions > 0).

Problems:

  1. Blocking: if the coordinator dies after PREPARE, participants hold locks until it recovers (they cannot decide alone). Orphaned prepared transactions pin the vacuum horizon and locks (a common outage cause).
  2. Latency: 2 round trips plus 2 durable writes per participant.
  3. Availability: every participant must be up.

Alternatives. Sagas (a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions, eventually consistent, app-level logic), outbox + idempotent consumers (file 06), or design so a transaction touches ONE shard (colocation).

Worked example. Booking = reserve seat (shard 1) + charge (payment service). With a saga: reserve seat (hold 10 min) then charge; if the charge fails, run the compensation "release seat". Visible intermediate states are accepted by design.

Industry examples. XA transactions in Java EE; Spanner and CockroachDB use 2PC internally, but over consensus groups (each "participant" is a replicated group, so it does not die as a single machine). Uber and most microservice shops prefer sagas.

Decision gravity. 2PC is a hard coupling of availability; sagas push complexity into application code. Hard to swap later, so decide at service-boundary design time.

Everyday analogy. A group dinner booking: the organiser asks everyone "can you make 8 pm and promise to keep it?" then only after all say yes announces "it is on".

Common interview traps.

  • Saying 2PC gives high availability. It reduces it.
  • Forgetting orphaned prepared transactions.
  • Calling a saga "atomic". It is eventually consistent with compensations.

notes.title: Raft and consensus-based SQL
notes.html:
Consensus protocols (Raft, Paxos) let a group of nodes agree on a single ordered log even when some fail, as long as a majority is alive. Distributed SQL databases replicate each data range through a consensus group, so a node dying does not lose committed data or require manual failover.

Raft in short:

  1. Nodes are leader, follower or candidate. One leader per term; if followers miss heartbeats (e.g. 150 to 300 ms randomised timeout) one becomes candidate and asks for votes; majority wins.
  2. Writes go to the leader, which appends to its log and replicates to followers.
  3. An entry is committed once a majority (e.g. 2 of 3, 3 of 5) has it durably; then it is applied and acknowledged.
  4. Tolerates f failures with 2f+1 nodes: 3 nodes tolerate 1, 5 tolerate 2.

Cost: every write needs a quorum round trip, so cross-region replication adds tens of ms (e.g. 60 to 150 ms between continents). Reads from the leader (or with leases) are linearizable.

Worked example. 3 replicas in 3 zones of one region (1 ms apart): write latency ~ 2 to 5 ms; a zone failure causes an election in ~1 to 3 s with no data loss. Spread over 3 regions: tolerates a full region loss, but writes pay ~ 80 to 150 ms.

Industry examples. etcd and Consul use Raft (Kubernetes' brain is etcd). CockroachDB, TiDB (TiKV), YugabyteDB use Raft per data range. Spanner uses Paxos groups.

Decision gravity. Choosing a consensus-backed database trades single-node write speed and operational familiarity for automatic failover and horizontal scale; moving back is a data migration.

Everyday analogy. A committee where a decision counts only when most members have signed; one absentee does not stop work.

Common interview traps.

  • Using an even number of nodes (4 tolerates the same as 3).
  • Claiming consensus is free. Each write waits for a quorum.
  • Mixing up replication-for-HA (Raft) with sharding (data partitioning); distributed SQL does both.

notes.title: Spanner, CockroachDB and distributed SQL
notes.html:
Distributed SQL databases look like one Postgres-like database but split tables into ranges, replicate each range with consensus, and run transactions across ranges with 2PC on top of that.

Google Spanner: globally distributed, externally consistent (strict serializable). Its trick is TrueTime: GPS and atomic clocks give a time interval with bounded uncertainty (single-digit ms). A transaction waits out the uncertainty ("commit wait") so timestamps order matches real time. Used for Google's ads and many internal systems; Cloud Spanner is the product.

CockroachDB: open-core, Postgres wire-compatible, serializable by default. No atomic clocks, so it uses hybrid logical clocks plus a maximum clock offset (default 500 ms) and read-uncertainty restarts. Ranges (~512 MB by default) are Raft groups; leases give fast leader reads. Features: multi-region tables (REGIONAL BY ROW), locality-aware replicas. Clients must retry 40001 errors.

Others: TiDB (MySQL-compatible, TiKV storage), YugabyteDB (Postgres-compatible query layer over DocDB), AlloyDB/Aurora (single-writer Postgres with a distributed storage layer, a different design), Citus (sharded Postgres, not consensus-based).

Worked example. A cross-region payments table: with REGIONAL BY ROW rows live in the user's home region (writes ~5 ms in-region), while a transfer between a US and an EU user spans two ranges and pays one cross-region 2PC round (~100+ ms, illustrative).

Trade-offs vs Postgres: higher latency per write (consensus), less mature extension and tool ecosystem, SQL feature differences, cost per node, and fewer tuning escape hatches. Gains: automatic rebalancing, online scale-out, survives zone or region loss.

Decision gravity. Moving to distributed SQL is a platform migration (drivers, retries, query tuning, ops). Do it for global multi-region writes or very large scale with strict consistency; do not adopt it just because "it scales".

Everyday analogy. A franchise with consistent rules in every branch, where every important decision needs several branches to sign off.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Spanner "beats CAP". It chooses consistency over availability during partitions, and makes partitions rare via private network and engineering.
  • Assuming wire compatibility means full Postgres compatibility.
  • Forgetting client retry logic.

notes.title: NoSQL families
notes.html:
NoSQL means non-relational stores that trade joins and general transactions for scale, flexibility or special access patterns. The families:

Family Model Examples Good for Weakness
Key-value key to blob Redis, DynamoDB, Riak Sessions, caches, carts, huge single-key throughput No ad-hoc queries
Wide-column rows with sparse column families, partition key + clustering key Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable, HBase Write-heavy time series, messaging, IoT Query-first modelling, limited joins
Document JSON documents MongoDB, Couchbase, Firestore Flexible schemas, aggregate-shaped data Cross-document transactions and joins weaker
Graph nodes and edges Neo4j, Neptune Relationship traversals (recommendations, fraud) Hard to shard
Search inverted index Elasticsearch, OpenSearch Full text, faceting, logs Not a system of record
Time series time-bucketed TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, ClickHouse (columnar OLAP) Metrics, analytics Updates/transactions limited

Worked example. Chat message history: 50B messages. Query is always "latest 50 for conversation X". A wide-column table with partition key conversation_id and clustering key message_time DESC serves this in one partition read (Discord's public engineering posts describe moving from Cassandra to ScyllaDB for this style of workload). Postgres could do it too to a point, then sharding is needed.

DynamoDB notes. Partition key + optional sort key; single-digit-ms latency at any scale; on-demand or provisioned capacity (a partition handles roughly 3,000 read and 1,000 write units/s, so hot keys throttle); GSIs for alternate access patterns; transactions limited in size.

Industry examples. Amazon cart (Dynamo paper), Netflix (Cassandra for large-scale data), Uber (Cassandra, MySQL-based Schemaless, later Docstore), LinkedIn (Espresso).

Decision gravity. Choosing NoSQL early locks you into a query model: new access patterns may mean a new table, a full backfill, or a different store. Postgres jsonb plus GIN indexes covers many "flexible schema" needs without leaving relational land.

Everyday analogy. Different containers: a toolbox, a filing cabinet, a shoe rack: each is superb at one job.

Common interview traps.

  • "NoSQL scales, SQL does not." Both scale; they trade different things.
  • Using MongoDB or Cassandra with a relational, join-heavy model.
  • Ignoring eventual consistency in Cassandra (tunable: QUORUM reads and writes give strong consistency per partition when R+W>N).

notes.title: LSM trees vs B-trees
notes.html:
Two storage-engine families. Postgres and InnoDB use B-trees: sorted pages updated in place, great for reads and range scans. Many NoSQL stores use LSM trees (log-structured merge): writes are cheap and sequential.

LSM write path:

  1. Append to a WAL (durability).
  2. Insert into an in-memory sorted memtable.
  3. When full (e.g. 64 MB), flush as an immutable sorted file (SSTable) on disk.
  4. Background compaction merges SSTables, dropping overwritten and deleted (tombstone) entries.

Read path: check memtable, then SSTables newest to oldest, using Bloom filters to skip files that cannot contain the key and block indexes to find it.

B-tree (Postgres) LSM (RocksDB, Cassandra)
Write Random page updates plus WAL Sequential appends
Read One path through the tree May check several files (Bloom filters help)
Write amplification Moderate Higher (compaction rewrites data, 10x or more)
Space Bloat from dead tuples Space amplification from old versions until compaction
Range scans Excellent Good (sorted), but across files

Worked example. Ingest 100,000 small writes/s of time-series. B-tree: each write dirties random pages and index pages, I/O bound. LSM: sequential WAL + memtable flushes, easily sustains it; cost shows up as background compaction I/O and read latency spikes if compaction falls behind.

Industry examples. RocksDB (embedded in CockroachDB's earlier storage engine Pebble lineage, TiKV, Kafka Streams state stores), LevelDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, Bigtable. Postgres alternatives like OrioleDB explore different engines.

Everyday analogy. LSM is tossing papers into an inbox and tidying in batches at night; a B-tree is filing each paper in the right drawer immediately.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying LSM is always faster. It wins on writes; reads and space can lose.
  • Forgetting tombstones and compaction when explaining deletes.

notes.title: CAP, PACELC and consistency models
notes.html:
CAP says that during a network partition a replicated system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets an answer). Partition tolerance is not optional in a real network, so the real choice is CP vs AP when partitions happen.

PACELC adds the normal-operation trade: Else (no partition) choose between Latency and Consistency. That is the more honest model: even healthy, synchronous replication costs latency.

Consistency spectrum: linearizable (strict) > serializable transaction semantics > causal > read-your-writes / monotonic reads > eventual.

System Typical stance
Postgres single node + sync replica CP-ish; availability drops if sync standby lost
Spanner, CockroachDB, etcd CP (PC/EC)
Cassandra, DynamoDB (default eventually consistent reads) AP-leaning, tunable
Redis with async replicas Can lose acknowledged writes on failover

Worked example. Shopping cart (Dynamo): during a partition keep accepting adds on both sides, merge later (available, eventual). Bank balance: refuse a withdrawal rather than risk overdraft (consistent).

Industry examples. Amazon's Dynamo paper (2007) popularised AP with vector clocks; Google Spanner made the CP case with engineering to keep availability high.

Everyday analogy. Two bank branches whose phone line is cut: either both stop serving until reconnected (consistent) or both keep serving and reconcile later (available).

Common interview traps.

  • Describing CAP as "pick any two".
  • Confusing ACID consistency with CAP consistency.
  • Ignoring the latency side of the trade (PACELC).

notes.title: When to leave Postgres, and when not to
notes.html:
Stay on Postgres until a measured limit says otherwise. It already does relational data, JSON (jsonb), full-text search, time series (TimescaleDB), geospatial (PostGIS), vectors (pgvector), queues (SKIP LOCKED) and pub/sub (LISTEN/NOTIFY). Fewer systems mean less operational risk.

Reasons to add or switch a store:

Signal Move
Cache-able hot reads at sub-ms, millions/s Add Redis (keep Postgres as truth)
Full-text relevance, faceting, log search Add Elasticsearch/OpenSearch fed by CDC
Massive analytics scans Warehouse or columnar (ClickHouse, BigQuery, Snowflake) fed by CDC
Write rate beyond one node, simple key access DynamoDB/Cassandra for that dataset
Strict multi-region writes Spanner/CockroachDB/YugabyteDB
Single huge tenant-partitioned dataset Shard (Citus/Vitess-like)
Event streaming between services Kafka

Worked example. E-commerce at 3,000 orders/min. Orders, inventory, payments: Postgres (ACID). Product search: Elasticsearch via CDC. Sessions and rate limits: Redis. Clickstream (200,000 events/s): Kafka to ClickHouse. Resist moving orders off Postgres; moving derived views is cheap, moving the source of truth is a one-way door.

Industry examples. Instagram, Notion, Figma and many unicorns ran on Postgres long past billions of rows, with partitioning and sharding when needed. Uber famously migrated from Postgres to MySQL in 2016 (public engineering post citing write amplification and replication issues of that era), showing it is workload and version specific, not a verdict on either database.

Decision gravity. Adding a derived store (cache, search, warehouse) is reversible: rebuild from the source. Replacing the source of truth is a multi-quarter migration with dual writes, backfills and verification.

Everyday analogy. Keep your main kitchen; add a blender or oven for specific dishes rather than rebuilding the house.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing a trendy store without naming the access pattern and number that forces it.
  • Having two sources of truth with dual writes and no reconciliation.
  • Forgetting migration cost: dual write, backfill, shadow read, cutover, rollback plan.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Climb the ladder: tune, scale up, replicas/cache, partition, functional split, shard, distributed SQL. Early steps are reversible; sharding is a one-way door.
  • Sharding needs a good shard key (high cardinality, in most queries); use logical shards; cross-shard joins, uniqueness and transactions become your problem.
  • 2PC gives atomicity across nodes but blocks and hurts availability; sagas and outbox trade atomicity for availability.
  • Raft/Paxos replicate logs with majority quorums (2f+1 nodes tolerate f failures); distributed SQL (Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, Yugabyte) shards into ranges, each a consensus group, with 2PC across ranges.
  • NoSQL families fit access patterns: key-value, wide-column, document, graph, search, time series.
  • LSM trees favour writes (memtable, SSTables, compaction, Bloom filters); B-trees favour reads and in-place updates.
  • CAP is about behaviour during partitions; PACELC adds latency vs consistency in normal operation.
  • Stay on Postgres until a measured limit; add derived stores via CDC; keep one source of truth.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between partitioning and sharding, and in what order would you reach for scaling options?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who jump to sharding at 100 GB are expensive. The signal is knowing the ladder and which steps are reversible.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Partitioning splits a table into pieces inside one database server; sharding splits it across several servers. I climb a ladder: fix queries and indexes, add pooling, scale up, add replicas and caching, partition, split by service, and only then shard. Steps up to partitioning and functional split are mostly reversible; sharding is a one-way door.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Tune -> Scale up -> Replicas/cache -> Partition -> Split by service -> Shard -> Distributed SQL
cheap, reversible  ------------------------------------------->  costly, one-way

A tuned 64-core, 512 GB NVMe Postgres handles tens of thousands of simple transactions per second and a few TB (illustrative; workload dependent). Real triggers to leave: write rate beyond one machine's WAL/fsync, working set not fitting RAM, vacuum or migrations on multi-TB tables taking too long, or needing local writes on several continents.

Partitioning keeps one transaction domain and makes vacuum, index builds and retention (drop a partition) cheap. Sharding changes every join, transaction, unique constraint and migration.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating partitioning and sharding.
  • Sharding for a read problem that replicas or caching would fix.
  • Not measuring before deciding.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does a functional split mean? -> Move a service's tables to their own database; still no shards.
  2. Why is sharding a one-way door? -> Application, queries and tooling become shard-aware.
  3. What numbers would convince you? -> Sustained write saturation after tuning, data beyond what one box can maintain.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "shard when the DB is big". Senior: orders options by reversibility, states measurable triggers, and uses real examples.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that sharded early spent quarters on cross-shard queries while a missing index was the real issue.

questions.promptHtml: Explain CAP and PACELC without saying "pick two of three".

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: CAP is the most misquoted theorem in interviews. They want precision.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CAP says that during a network partition a replicated system must choose between consistency and availability; since partitions happen, the real choice is CP versus AP when they do. PACELC adds that even with no partition you trade latency against consistency, because synchronous coordination costs time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Consistency here means linearizability (every read sees the latest write), not ACID's consistency. Availability means every non-failing node answers.

Partition -> choose C: reject or wait (CP)
Partition -> choose A: serve possibly stale data, reconcile later (AP)
No partition -> choose L (fast, async) or C (wait for replicas)
System Stance
Postgres + sync standby CP-ish; writes block if sync standby lost
Spanner, CockroachDB, etcd CP
Cassandra, DynamoDB eventual reads AP leaning, tunable
Redis with async replicas Can lose acknowledged writes on failover

Example: a cart keeps accepting adds on both sides of a partition and merges later (AP); a bank refuses a withdrawal it cannot verify (CP).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Pick any two".
  • Confusing ACID C with CAP C.
  • Ignoring the latency half (PACELC).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Spanner beat CAP? -> No; it is CP and makes partitions rare via private network and engineering.
  2. Cassandra with QUORUM reads and writes? -> R+W>N gives strong consistency per partition, at lower availability.
  3. Where does single-node Postgres sit? -> No partitions to tolerate, so CAP is not the relevant lens.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average recites the triangle. Senior ties it to concrete systems, tunable consistency, and the latency trade.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Failover with async replication turns "available" into "lost acknowledged writes" and surprises teams.

questions.promptHtml: How do you choose between key-value, wide-column, document, graph and search stores?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They want an access-pattern-driven answer, not brand names.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I start from the access pattern. Key lookups at huge throughput point to key-value; massive write streams read by a partition key point to wide-column; aggregate-shaped flexible JSON points to document; relationship traversal to graph; full text and faceting to a search engine. If I need ad-hoc relational queries and transactions I stay on Postgres.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Family Fits Weak at
Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB) Sessions, carts, single-key throughput Ad-hoc queries
Wide-column (Cassandra, Scylla, Bigtable) Time series, messaging, write-heavy Joins, new access patterns
Document (MongoDB) Flexible schemas Cross-document joins/transactions
Graph (Neo4j) Recommendations, fraud Sharding
Search (Elasticsearch) Text, facets, logs System of record

Example: chat history "latest 50 messages for conversation X": wide-column with partition key conversation_id and clustering message_time DESC serves it in one partition read. Modelling is query-first: new queries can mean new tables and backfills.

Also note Postgres jsonb plus GIN covers many flexible-schema needs.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "NoSQL scales, SQL does not".
  • Join-heavy models on MongoDB or Cassandra.
  • Forgetting eventual consistency defaults.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is Cassandra modelling query-first? -> Data is partitioned by key; queries not on the key scatter or are unsupported.
  2. Can search be the source of truth? -> Not advisable; derive it via CDC.
  3. When does jsonb suffice? -> Moderate scale with ad-hoc filters and transactions needed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists products. Senior names the access pattern, number and the migration cost of being wrong.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams adopting a document store for relational data rebuilt joins in application code, slower than Postgres.

questions.contextHtml: A B2B SaaS has 4 TB across 6,000 tenants; the top tenant is 9% of rows and the top 10 are 35%. Queries: 85% are per-tenant, 10% are admin-wide reports, 5% are cross-tenant joins for partner features. Writes: 12,000/s. Proposed keys: user_id hash, tenant_id hash, created_at range, and country. Target: no shard above 500 GB.
questions.promptHtml: Which shard key and strategy do you pick?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Hash user_id for even distribution". It makes most per-tenant queries scatter-gather.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are transactions within a tenant? Can big tenants grow without bound? Is data residency a factor? Are tenant IDs in every query?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I'd first confirm we cannot get by with partitioning plus replicas at 4 TB.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: tenant_id fits 85% of queries and keeps transactions local; created_at hot-spots the newest shard; country skews; user_id scatters tenant queries.
  4. How I'd verify: Query log analysis for the predicate on each table; tenant size distribution histogram.
  5. Root cause (of the risk): The top tenant at 9% of 4 TB is 360 GB, nearly a whole shard, so pure hash by tenant is lumpy.
  6. Fix: Directory-based or logical-shard mapping on tenant_id: for example 64 logical shards on 8 hosts, and a lookup that places mega tenants on dedicated shards. Colocate all tenant tables:
SELECT create_distributed_table('orders', 'tenant_id');
SELECT create_distributed_table('order_items', 'tenant_id', colocate_with => 'orders');

Admin reports run on a CDC-fed warehouse; partner joins go through an API or a replicated reference table. 7. Prevention: Per-shard size and QPS dashboards; rebalancing runbook; ID scheme not dependent on shard-local auto-increment (Snowflake/UUIDv7). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Directory is a critical dependency, so cache it and replicate it. I would not shard on created_at.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Tenant 1 grows to 2 TB? -> Needs sub-sharding within the tenant or a dedicated cluster.
  • Need global unique email? -> Separate global index table or lookup service.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team hashed on a celebrity-heavy user key; one shard ran at 95% CPU while the others idled.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks a key without looking at queries.
  • Hire: tenant_id with justification and hash/logical shards.
  • Strong hire: handles mega tenants, colocation, reports, and ID generation.

questions.contextHtml:
An internal XA-style coordinator performs transfers across two Postgres databases. At 14:05 the coordinator host was OOM-killed mid-run. By 14:40: table bloat alarm, a few updates hang, and autovacuum does not shrink dead tuples.

 gid          | prepared            | owner
 tx-8841      | 2026-11-09 14:05:11 | app
 tx-8849      | 2026-11-09 14:05:12 | app
SHOW max_prepared_transactions;  -> 100
oldest xmin age: 12.4M and growing

Red herring: someone blames a recent index migration.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart Postgres" (prepared transactions survive a restart) or killing connections (they have none).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are all prepared transactions from the same coordinator? Does the coordinator log the decision?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Resolve the prepared transactions: for each, check the coordinator's decision log and run COMMIT PREPARED 'gid' or ROLLBACK PREPARED 'gid'.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) orphaned prepared transactions holding locks and xmin, (b) a long idle transaction, (c) the index migration (check timing: no).
  4. How I'd verify: SELECT * FROM pg_prepared_xacts; and pg_locks joined on the virtual transaction; compare with pg_stat_activity.
  5. Root cause: After PREPARE a participant must wait for the decision; the coordinator died before sending it, so locks and the vacuum horizon are pinned.
  6. Fix: Recover per decision log; if the log is lost, consistency needs checking per participant (if any participant committed, commit the others). Longer term: a recovery daemon at coordinator start, timeouts, alerting on pg_prepared_xacts age.
  7. Prevention: Prefer a design where a transaction touches one shard, or a saga with compensation; limit max_prepared_transactions to what is needed.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not blind-rollback everything: a transaction already committed on another participant would break atomicity.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Coordinator log lost? -> Inspect each participant's state; commit if any committed, otherwise rollback after business check.
  • Why not sagas? -> Possible, at the cost of visible intermediate states and compensation logic.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a forgotten prepared transaction held the xmin horizon for four days, bloating a hot table until performance collapsed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts the database.
  • Hire: finds via pg_prepared_xacts and resolves with the coordinator log.
  • Strong hire: explains blocking property, alerts, and alternatives like sagas.

questions.contextHtml:
After sharding orders into 4 Postgres shards by hash(customer_id) % 4, these bugs reached production within a week.

# routing
def shard_for(customer_id):
    return hash(customer_id) % 4      # Python's built-in hash on str

# id generation (each shard has its own SERIAL starting at 1)
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total) VALUES (%s, %s) RETURNING id;

# admin page
for shard in shards:
    rows += shard.query("SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50")
return rows[:50]

# lookup by order id
shard = shard_for(order_id)

Symptoms: customers see someone else's order on /orders/17; some customers' data vanished after a deploy; the admin list misses recent rows and order is odd. Red herring: a team member suspects replication lag.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Finds one bug (the admin merge) and misses the routing and ID issues.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which language/runtime versions? Did the deploy change PYTHONHASHSEED? Is order_id globally unique?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause writes to the router, restore the stable routing function, and flag orders affected.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) built-in hash() of strings is randomised per process, so the same customer maps to different shards after restart; (b) per-shard SERIAL means id=17 exists on all four shards and shard_for(order_id) routes by the wrong key; (c) the admin merge takes top 50 per shard then slices without sorting the merged result.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare shard_for output across two process restarts; query SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id=17 on each shard; check the final slice sorting.
  5. Root cause: Unstable hash function, non-global IDs, and a wrong scatter-gather merge.
  6. Fix:
import hashlib
def shard_for(customer_id: str, n_logical=64):
    h = int(hashlib.sha1(customer_id.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
    return h % n_logical          # logical shard -> host via mapping table

# id: Snowflake/UUIDv7 with shard bits embedded, so order_id routes itself
rows = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r.created_at, reverse=True)[:50]

Reconcile misrouted rows with a one-off migration. 7. Prevention: Test that routing is deterministic across processes; global ID generator; contract tests for scatter-gather. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Embedding shard in the ID speeds lookups but ties IDs to topology; logical shards soften that. I would not blame replication lag.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Admin page needs offset pagination? -> Use keyset pagination per shard and merge.
  • Secondary index on email? -> Lookup table or global index.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a deploy upgraded the runtime and changed hash seeding; a fifth of customers' rows landed on the "wrong" shard until a backfill fixed them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames replication lag.
  • Hire: finds unstable hash and duplicate IDs.
  • Strong hire: also fixes merge, introduces logical shards and tests for determinism.

questions.promptHtml: How does two-phase commit work, why is it avoided across services, and what do you use instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests distributed-transaction fundamentals and the ability to choose an alternative with eyes open.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In 2PC a coordinator asks every participant to PREPARE, meaning make the transaction durable and promise it can commit; if all say yes it logs the decision and sends COMMIT, otherwise ABORT. The problem is blocking: if the coordinator dies after PREPARE, participants hold locks until it returns. It also adds round trips and requires all participants up. Instead I use sagas with compensating actions, or an outbox with idempotent consumers, or design so a transaction stays within one shard.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Coordinator        A          B
PREPARE ---------> yes(durable)
PREPARE ---------------------> yes(durable)
log decision
COMMIT ----------> done
COMMIT ---------------------->  done

Costs: two network round trips plus two durable writes per participant; availability equals the product of all participants' availability. Postgres: PREPARE TRANSACTION, COMMIT PREPARED, needs max_prepared_transactions > 0; orphans pin locks and vacuum.

Sagas: seat reserved (hold 10 minutes), then payment; on failure run "release seat". The system is eventually consistent and intermediate states are visible by design. Spanner and CockroachDB do use 2PC internally, but each participant is a replicated consensus group, so it does not die as one machine.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying 2PC improves availability.
  • Calling a saga atomic.
  • Forgetting idempotency in saga steps and compensations.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if a compensation fails? -> Retry idempotently, with alerts and manual queue.
  2. Where does the outbox fit? -> Atomically write the event with the data, publish later; consumers dedupe.
  3. Why does distributed SQL make 2PC tolerable? -> Participants are Raft groups, so a leader loss recovers quickly.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: describes prepare/commit. Senior: blocking, orphan handling, availability maths, saga design with idempotency.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash between PREPARE and COMMIT is the cause of many "locks never released" incidents.

questions.contextHtml: A DynamoDB table events (partition key date, e.g. "2026-11-09", sort key event_id) is provisioned at 20,000 WCU. At peak the app receives ProvisionedThroughputExceededException while CloudWatch shows consumed capacity at only 4,000 WCU, about 20% of provisioned. Writes: 5,000/s all stamped with today's date. Red herring: the team suspects the SDK retry config.
questions.promptHtml: Why is it throttling and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise the provisioned capacity." Total capacity is not the limit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the partition key? Distribution of keys? Reads by date needed? Is adaptive capacity on?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable on-demand mode or write-shard temporarily; reduce bursts; backoff with jitter.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) hot partition: every write goes to one key, and one partition handles roughly 1,000 write units/s (verify current limits), (b) SDK retries (symptom, not cause), (c) large items.
  4. How I'd verify: CloudWatch contributor insights / throttled requests by key; check key cardinality.
  5. Root cause: A low-cardinality partition key concentrates all writes on one partition.
  6. Fix: Write-shard the key: date#shard with shard in 0..N-1 (N about 10 to 20), and read by querying all shards and merging. Or choose a high-cardinality key like device_id with a GSI for date queries.
import random
pk = f"{date}#{random.randrange(16)}"
  1. Prevention: Key design review with expected QPS per key; alarms on throttled requests; load test with realistic skew.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sharded keys make date reads fan out 16 queries; acceptable for batch consumers. I would not keep raising capacity.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can't change the table? -> Create a new table and migrate with dual write and backfill.
  • Adaptive capacity? -> Helps with skew over time but not a single hot key beyond partition limits.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team keyed by tenant and one tenant imported 50M records, throttling its writes while the others were fine.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases capacity.
  • Hire: identifies hot key and write-shards.
  • Strong hire: quantifies partition limits, plans migration, and sets key-design reviews.

questions.promptHtml: How does Raft commit a write, and why do you run 3 or 5 nodes rather than 4?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Consensus underlies etcd, CockroachDB and TiKV; they want mechanism and sizing logic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: One leader per term appends the write to its log and replicates it to followers; once a majority has it durably, the entry is committed and acknowledged. The group tolerates f failures with 2f+1 nodes, so 3 tolerate one and 5 tolerate two. A fourth node adds cost but still tolerates only one failure, since a majority of 4 is 3.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Client -> Leader -> Follower 1
          Leader -> Follower 2
majority ack (leader + 1 of 2) -> committed -> applied

Election: followers that miss heartbeats within a randomised timeout (for example 150 to 300 ms) become candidates and ask for votes; a majority wins; randomisation avoids split votes. A leader without a majority steps down, so a minority partition cannot commit, which is why it is CP.

Latency: every write waits for a quorum round trip. Three zones in one region (1 ms apart) means write latency of a few ms; three regions makes it 80 to 150 ms. Reads from the leader (with leases) are linearizable. A zone failure triggers an election in about 1 to 3 seconds without data loss.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Even node counts.
  • Believing consensus is free.
  • Confusing replication for HA with sharding.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why odd sizes? -> Same fault tolerance as the next lower odd size, more network cost.
  2. What happens in a 2-3 partition of 5 nodes? -> The 3-side keeps committing, the 2-side stalls.
  3. Can a follower serve reads? -> Only with follower reads or read-index at the cost of staleness or extra checks.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average states "majority". Senior discusses terms, election timeouts, leader step-down and latency maths across regions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An etcd cluster with slow disks causes missed heartbeats, constant elections and Kubernetes control plane instability.

questions.contextHtml:
A payments service moved from Postgres to a 9-node CockroachDB cluster across us-east, eu-west and ap-south (3 nodes each), default replica placement, serializable isolation. After the move: p50 write 4 ms became 140 ms; p99 under contention 2.5 s; clients log restart transaction: TransactionRetryWithProtoRefreshError (SQLSTATE 40001) about 3% of the time; a hot "balance summary" row is updated by many transactions.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE: ... round trips to leaseholder in eu-west for rows owned by US users

Red herring: someone says "CPU is only 20%, so the cluster has headroom".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more nodes." Latency comes from quorum across regions and contention, not capacity.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where do users live? What are the survival goals (zone or region)? Are transactions single-row or multi-row? Is the summary row on the critical path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add client-side retry for 40001 with backoff (mandatory), and move the summary update out of the hot path.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) replicas spread over three regions so every write needs a cross-region quorum (60 to 150 ms), (b) leaseholders far from the user, (c) a hot row producing read/write conflicts and restarts, (d) cross-region 2PC for transfers between regions.
  4. How I'd verify: SHOW RANGES/range placement, DB console latency per locality, crdb_internal contention events.
  5. Root cause: Default placement optimised for region-level survival at the price of write latency; plus contention on one row.
  6. Fix: REGIONAL BY ROW tables so each user's rows live and lease in their home region (in-region writes about 5 to 10 ms); SURVIVE ZONE FAILURE where region survival is not required; replace the hot balance row with append-only ledger rows and an async aggregate; client retries.
ALTER TABLE accounts SET LOCALITY REGIONAL BY ROW;
ALTER DATABASE payments SURVIVE ZONE FAILURE;
  1. Prevention: Contention dashboards; retry wrapper in the data layer; load tests per region; define survivability goals explicitly.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Cross-region transfers still pay a 2PC round. Region survival costs latency, so decide per table.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Are clocks a factor? -> Clock offset bounds (default max 500 ms, verify) and read uncertainty restarts matter on high skew.
  • Is Postgres compatibility complete? -> No; test extensions, locking behaviour and query plans.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: an app without 40001 retry handling turned a 3% retry rate into customer-visible failures; a retry wrapper fixed it in a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds nodes.
  • Hire: explains quorum latency, retries and regional placement.
  • Strong hire: addresses contention redesign, survivability trade-off and compatibility testing.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how an LSM tree handles writes and reads, and when you would choose it over a B-tree.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It reveals whether you understand storage engines beneath Cassandra, RocksDB and Postgres, not just API behavior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An LSM writes to a WAL and an in-memory memtable, flushes sorted immutable SSTables, and compacts them in the background. Writes are sequential and cheap; reads may touch several files, helped by Bloom filters. A B-tree updates pages in place: better point reads and range scans, but random IO on writes. I choose LSM for write-heavy ingest like time series and messaging, and B-tree for read-heavy general OLTP.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Write -> WAL -> Memtable -> flush SSTable (L0) -> compaction -> sorted levels L1..Ln
Read  -> memtable -> SSTables newest to oldest (Bloom filter skips files)
B-tree LSM
Write Random page updates + WAL Sequential appends
Read One path Several files
Write amplification Moderate High (compaction rewrites, 10x+ typical, verify per config)
Space Dead tuples bloat Old versions until compaction
Delete Mark dead, vacuum Tombstone until compaction

100,000 small writes/s overwhelm a B-tree's random IO but suit an LSM; the cost shows up as compaction IO and read latency spikes if compaction falls behind.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "LSM is always faster".
  • Forgetting tombstones, which cost reads until compacted.
  • Ignoring write amplification on SSD lifespan.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do Bloom filters buy? -> They skip SSTables that definitely lack the key; false positives only cost an extra read.
  2. Leveled vs size-tiered compaction? -> Leveled: lower read and space amplification, higher write amplification; size-tiered the opposite.
  3. Why do deletes hurt? -> Tombstones must be read and survive until compaction passes the retention window.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "LSM faster writes". Senior: amplification trade-offs, compaction strategy and operational failure modes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Cassandra cluster with heavy deletes and queues suffered tombstone scan timeouts until the model changed.

questions.contextHtml:
A 12-node Cassandra cluster ingests 150,000 writes/s of sensor data. After a marketing spike doubled ingestion, read p99 went from 8 ms to 900 ms, and disk usage climbs 4% per hour. nodetool shows:

Pending compactions: 1,840
SSTables per read (p99): 38
Write latency: normal (2 ms)
Disk: 78% used, compaction output needs space

Red herring: GC pauses look normal, and CPU is 55%.
questions.promptHtml: What is going on and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a cache" or "restart nodes", which makes compaction worse.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Compaction strategy? Disk type and throughput limits? TTL/delete mix? Can the spike be throttled?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce incoming rate if possible (backpressure), raise compaction_throughput temporarily if IO allows, and free disk headroom before it hits the danger point where compaction cannot complete.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) compaction backlog: reads must merge 38 SSTables, (b) disk IO saturation, (c) tombstones, (d) GC (checked, normal).
  4. How I'd verify: nodetool compactionstats, iostat -x, cfstats tombstones per read.
  5. Root cause: Write rate exceeded compaction capacity, so SSTable count grew; LSM defers the cost of writes to background work, and the debt came due as read amplification.
  6. Fix: Short term: throttle writes, increase compaction capacity, add nodes (bootstrapping adds load, so do it carefully). Long term: time-window compaction for time series with TTLs, capacity plan for write amplification, faster disks, scale out before sustained utilisation passes about 50% of IO capacity (rule of thumb, verify).
  7. Prevention: Alert on pending compactions and SSTables per read; load test at 2x peak; maintain disk headroom (size-tiered needs up to 50%).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not run a major compaction on all nodes at once, nor delete data files.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why are writes still fast? -> Writes only touch the WAL and memtable; the pain is deferred to reads.
  • Switch to TWCS now? -> Only with a tested plan; it changes how existing data is handled.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: an LSM-based store looked fine for months until a backfill produced a compaction backlog that took nine days to drain.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds caching or restarts.
  • Hire: ties read latency to SSTable count and compaction.
  • Strong hire: disk headroom risk, compaction strategy choice, load tests and alerts.

questions.contextHtml: A 6 TB orders table lives on 4 shards (hash(customer_id) % 4, no logical shards). Each shard hits 85% disk and 70% CPU; growth is 12% per month. Business wants no downtime beyond 30 s and no lost writes. Moving to 8 shards by changing the modulus would relocate about half of the data, and the app has the shard count hard-coded in 14 services.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Take a maintenance window and rehash everything." It violates the downtime limit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which queries cross shards? Are there background writers? Can we introduce a routing layer first? How much read lag is tolerable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Buy time: archive cold data, add disk, partition old data, so the migration is not rushed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Main risks: hard-coded modulus, consistency during copy, validation, rollback.
  4. How I'd verify: Row counts and checksums per key range; shadow reads comparing old and new shards.
  5. Root cause (of the pain): Direct modulus sharding ties placement to the shard count.
  6. Fix: Plan: (1) introduce a routing layer/library with a logical-shard map (for example 256 virtual shards; today's 4 hosts own 64 each) with no data movement; (2) for each virtual shard to move, copy via logical replication or snapshot plus CDC to the new host; (3) dual-write or rely on CDC until lag is near zero; (4) shadow read and compare; (5) briefly pause writes for that virtual shard (seconds), flip the map entry, resume; (6) keep the reverse stream for rollback; repeat in small batches.
  7. Prevention: Always shard into logical shards; automation and dashboards for per-shard size; rehearse.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dual writes without reconciliation create two truths; I use CDC from a single source and verify. I would not move all virtual shards at once.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A move fails halfway? -> Map entry never flipped, so the old shard stays authoritative; discard the copy.
  • Cross-shard transactions during the flip? -> Pause only that virtual shard and drain in-flight transactions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team moved virtual shards 5 per night for two weeks; each flip took under 10 seconds and nobody outside the platform team noticed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: maintenance window rehash.
  • Hire: logical shards, copy plus CDC, flip.
  • Strong hire: verification, rollback path, small batches, and routing layer first.

questions.contextHtml: The CTO says: "We keep getting slow and need to scale; let's move to Cassandra or Cockroach." Facts you find: Postgres 15 on one 16-core, 128 GB node, 1.1 TB data, 1,800 writes/s peak, 9,000 reads/s. A top query does a seq scan on a 300M-row table, 2,400 connections open directly from the app, one 4 TB reporting join runs hourly on the primary, and p99 is 1.8 s. Replicas: none. Last quarter's outages were related to connection exhaustion.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Agrees to a platform migration, or says "Postgres cannot scale".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the SLO and which user journeys are slow? What growth do we expect? Any multi-region requirement? Do we have a measured limit that Postgres reached?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add pooling (PgBouncer) and the missing index, move reporting to a replica.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) a missing index plus a seq scan on 300M rows, (b) connection overload, (c) reports competing with OLTP, (d) real write ceiling (1,800 writes/s is far below a single node's limit).
  4. How I'd verify: pg_stat_statements for top time, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), pg_stat_activity, cache hit ratio, IO wait.
  5. Root cause: Operational and query-level issues, not a data-model or scale ceiling.
  6. Fix: Index and query fixes, pooling, a read replica for reports, caching hot reads if needed, partition the 300M-row table by time. Re-evaluate after measuring; if a real trigger appears (multi-region writes, 10x write growth), consider add-on stores or distributed SQL for that dataset only.
  7. Prevention: Capacity model with explicit thresholds that would trigger the next step; regular query review; a decision record for the ladder.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Switching the source of truth is a multi-quarter migration with dual writes, backfills, shadow reads and cutover; I would not take that risk without a measured limit. Distributed SQL would add latency per write.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if we truly need three-region writes? -> Then distributed SQL such as Spanner or CockroachDB is justified for that data.
  • And search relevance? -> Add Elasticsearch as a derived store via CDC.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team spent two quarters on a NoSQL migration, then discovered a missing composite index had caused the original slowness; the new system needed the same index logic.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: agrees to migrate or declares Postgres cannot scale.
  • Hire: diagnoses with data, applies the ladder.
  • Strong hire: names triggers that would justify a move, covers migration cost and keeps one source of truth.
